Houses with female occupants outside.
House with some decoration.
A dilapidated rectilinear house showing walling made from vertically placed drinks cans, mortared and plastered over with mud.

Cartons of sorghum beer (Chibuku brand) stacked together and used as firewood. The typical way of burning logs was end-on in this manner, pushing them gradually further inwards as they burned down. Since the population of Maun had increased, firewood was impossible to find close to the town centre, and people would need to go further and further afield to collect it. This meant that some people has to burn waste in this way to survive.
Christopher Morton with a family in Matlapaneng Ward in Maun.
Model of Ngwato (Tswana) woman with child on her back.
Portrait of two women, one wearing the membership badge of the ZCC (Zionist Christian Church).

A partially built / dilapidated structure, showing use of thin concrete blocks in a similar manner to mud bricks, still retaining wooden corner posts for roof support. Not having enough of this material to make the entire structure, the rest of the walling is made from reeds.
Models of three seated men holding skins; in discussion. Caption reads: 'Ba-mangwatu men working karosses, mantles made from skins of game'.
A concrete block thatched rondavel and a concrete block two-roomed house, in a compound in Maun.
View of a house designed as two conjoined concrete-block structures, with separate entrances, probably built at different times.
Concrete block house with letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) lolwapa courtyard fence.
View of homestead in Maun, including huts with letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) to right, and concrete to left. Hut in centre is being re-roofed.
Decorative entrance to a hut made from bottles sunk into the sand in the shape of a heart. In the homestead of Mma Keabetswe Sefo in Saphane Ward.
A man and a child playing the traditional Mancala-style game Serobaroba, with four rows and sixteen holes scooped out of the sand.
A rectilinear hut with tin roof (ntlo ya plata) and walling made from bundles of grass.
A courtyard inside a lolwapa where cooking takes place, with a rectilinear hut to left using drinks cans as a walling material.
Two rectilinear huts using different techniques; in the foreground a mud-brick hut with tin roof, and beyond using wooden exterior posts to support a thatched roof.
Tree stumps showing the felling of mopane trees for building and firewood by local inhabitants.
Small children playing in a passageway created between outer and inner fencing in a homestead belonging to Mma Lebela.
A homestead view showing round huts made from mud-plastered poles and a tree planted for shade and medicinal use.
Poles of stripped mopane wood stacked in readiness for building.
Plot fenced with wooden poles and wire.
Mopane cutting and coppicing.
Circular hut under construction, partly thatched and walling of mud bricks and a course of drinks cans from local bars incorporated.

Closer view of rectilinear hut under construction made using mopane poles for roof support and rafters and drinks cans plastered in mud. The drinks cans are being reused from the hut that fell down after the rains. A small fireplace is being used within. In the homestead of Kgosilebatho Letsile.
Homestead with sapling planted in the foreground for shade and medicinal purposes. The sapling is heavily protected from animals.
Woman rinsing clothes in a tub during a heavy rain storm.
A lean-to shelter for cooking beside a hut, incorporating corrugated tin, wild sage stems, and a metal barrel beaten flat.
A woman in her small field, around which she has created a hedge of cut mopane bush branches (maphanyane), to keep goats away.
A small field, around which a hedge has been made of cut mopane bush branches (maphanyane), to keep goats away.

A homestead in Maun, with a European style house to left (ntlo ya sekgoa) and a relatively unusual example of a circular building made from concrete bricks and conical thatch roof. Most families, if they managed to buy concrete bricks, would build square and roof it with sheets of corrugated tin (disenke).
Hut with mud brick walls and base incorporating drinks cans. Part of the wall is augmented with letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) and grasses.
Hut with walls made from loose wooden staves.

Two rectilinear huts, one with drinks-can and mud walling, joined by a lethlaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) courtyard fence. One of the huts is roofed with grass thatch, the other with sheets of corrugated iron. In the homestead of Mma Keabetswe Sefo in Saphane Ward.
A goat enclosure around a tree made from wooden staves and an iron sheet gate. Next to the homestead of Mma Keabetswe Sefo in Saphane Ward.
A concrete block house under construction. Such houses are sometimes described as 'ntlo ya sekgoa', a European house. In the homestead of Mma Keabetswe Sefo in Saphane Ward.
Female friends chatting on a concrete seat made around a tree, in Wenela Ward.
Female friends chatting on a concrete seat made around a tree, in Wenela Ward.
A rectilinear hut with tin roof (ntlo ya plata) and walling plastered with concrete.
Tree stump showing the felling of mopane trees for building and firewood by local inhabitants.
View of a homestead, with a felled tree used for firewood in the foreground.
A field fenced using available wood and branches gathered from the surrounding area.
House under construction, using drinks cans from a local bar. In the homestead of Seekapo Mapororo.

A member of the Bakomoso Weaving Cooperative in Shorobe village (Boipuso Nyope) showing some land set aside by the weavers to plant palm as well as plants that produce dyes for weaving, so that other people will not cut them down.
Small children playing in a passageway created between outer and inner fencing in a homestead belonging to Mma Lebela.
Small children playing in a passageway created between outer and inner fencing in a homestead belonging to Mma Lebela.
Negatives from fieldwork in Ngamiland, 1999-2000. Awaiting detailed cataloguing.
A rectilinear hut built square to use tin roofing, with walling made from poles plastered over with mud.
Mopane showing some trunks having been cut and other new growths left for future cutting.
Mopane coppicing.
Mopane cutting and coppicing.
A small goat pen (lesaka) made from mopane poles. A concrete toilet ("long drop") is visible in the background. In the homestead of Kgosilebatho Letsile.
A pollarded mopane tree in a homestead, with a concrete block building in the background.
A small wind-break shelter used for cooking, using old letlhaka for walling (water reeds, Phragmites australis).
A coppiced mopane tree.
A pollarded mopane tree.
Plastic sheeting used to make grass thatch roofs more waterproof during the rains.

Stacks of letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) leaning against the courtyard fence (lolwapa) made from the same, at the home of Ghana Zambo in Mabadutsa ward. Letlhaka was increasingly expensive to buy in Maun since it was only found deep in the delta swamps, and people needed to pay for transport or collection.
